title: "Escalation: what has to reach you, and how fast"

## The ticket

Tuesday, 11:52 p.m. Your phone rings. It's your Quality Analyst (QA), and she doesn't sound
like someone asking permission — she sounds like someone handing you information she's already
decided you need. Riverside General Hospital just called her: a transfusion recipient has died,
and the unit involved may be one of Lakeshore's. She hasn't determined anything yet. She isn't
asking what to do. She's telling you it happened, now, because she already decided this isn't a
call that waits for morning.

She's right — and by the time your alarm goes off Wednesday, four more decisions exactly like
that one will have been made that night, by her or by whoever's covering the on-call phone: is
this an event that needs you immediately, needs you today, or can wait for your next
one-on-one? Some of the calls that night are easy. One of them is built to test whether she has
anywhere to go if the pressure *not* to escalate turns out to be coming from somewhere close to
you.

This module is about how she makes that call before anything is confirmed — and how you'd make
it yourself, at 2 a.m., with nothing but a first report and five minutes to decide.

## Why this matters — and the ITIL bridge

You already run a version of this every day. ITIL's major-incident criteria and priority matrix
exist so "is this bad enough to wake someone up" isn't reinvented every time something breaks —
the criteria are agreed in advance, the matrix scores impact and urgency, and a published
on-call runbook already names who gets called, in what order, before the incident happens. You
also already know **functional escalation** (routing sideways, to whoever owns the function that
needs to act) from **hierarchical escalation** (routing upward, to someone with more authority).
And you know an escalation path written *after* the fire starts is worthless.

All of that still applies tonight. Three things push past what your normal incident model was
built for.

**An external regulatory clock can already be running before anyone escalates internally, and
it doesn't wait for your investigation.** FDA's clock on a reportable biological product
deviation starts the moment someone acquires information *"reasonably suggesting"* a reportable
event occurred — not the moment anyone confirms one did. Criteria built to fire on confirmation
quietly give away days of a clock you didn't know was running.

**Some escalations have to bypass the line manager on purpose.** The on-call engineer normally
escalates up the chain they report through. Here, the person applying quality judgment sometimes
has to escalate *around* the reporting line she sits in, because the pressure not to escalate can
come from inside it. Your ITSM world guards against a manager overruling technical judgment with
better information. This world has to guard against a manager suppressing quality judgment with
neither.

**The decision owner for a product isn't the incident commander.** On a product-safety
escalation, your job stops at making sure the right person hears about it fast enough to
decide — that's Quality or the medical director, not you, and not IT. `quality-system-essentials`
already showed this working: the Owen Pruitt donation's 7:50 a.m. doorway conversation, a verbal
escalation before any write-up existed, was already this in miniature. This module gives that
instinct a name, a set of tiers, and a clock.

## The rule in plain English

**Escalation criteria are a written, pre-agreed artifact — not a judgment call made fresh each
time.** Same discipline QSE taught for an effectiveness check: the criterion is set *before* the
event, not reverse-engineered afterward to justify whatever someone already decided. A QA
inventing the threshold at 11:52 p.m. is doing her hardest thinking under the worst conditions.
Agree the criteria with Quality and IT leadership in daylight, and the 2 a.m. decision becomes
"which bucket does this fall in," not "how bad does this feel right now."

**Four tiers.**

| Tier | What it means | Roughly |
|---|---|---|
| **Call me now** | Reaches you immediately, any hour, by phone. | A clock may already be running, or the situation could still get worse in real time. |
| **Tell me today** | Reaches you the same business day, doesn't have to interrupt sleep. | Real, needs your attention soon, isn't actively unfolding. |
| **Your call, tell me at our one-on-one** | She decides whether it needs you at all; if it does, your regular check-in is soon enough. | Low severity, already contained, or squarely inside her own decision rights. |
| **Periodic report** | No individual routing at all — it rolls into a scheduled metric or trend. | Aggregate patterns (aging, recurrence rate) that only mean something in volume, not as single events. |

**Eight trigger categories cover most of what actually needs a "now" or "today" tier:**

- Possible patient harm or a fatality, confirmed or not
- Distributed product that may affect safety
- A consignee notification or retrieval question (21 CFR 606.100(b)(19) — Lakeshore's SOPs must
  include procedures for notifying consignees; what actually triggers that duty is in 610.46 and
  610.47, which this course doesn't teach — name the category, don't chase it deeper)
- A regulatory clock that has started, or plausibly has
- A suspected breach of donor or patient data — a category only; notification rules and clocks
  after a confirmed breach belong to a future course (`healthcare-security-and-privacy`)
- A BECS (Blood Establishment Computer Software) critical-function failure or a break in its
  validated state
- A regulator or assessor on site, or any regulatory correspondence arriving
- Pressure on a quality decision, from any direction

**Functional vs. hierarchical escalation, applied here.** Functional escalation routes to
whoever owns the function implicated, regardless of org chart — a suspected data breach goes to
the privacy/security owner whether or not that person reports anywhere near you. Hierarchical
escalation routes upward for authority. Most real escalations need both at once: a fatality call
needs the medical director functionally (clinical and regulatory judgment is theirs) *and* you
hierarchically (you need to know, and you may need to preserve IT evidence only you control).

**Who it goes past the Director to.** You are not the ceiling on any of this. Depending on the
category, the event needs to reach someone else directly — sometimes instead of you, sometimes
alongside you, never gated on you first if speed matters more than sequence:

| Category | Goes to | Why not just you |
|---|---|---|
| Product, donor, or patient safety | Medical director | Disposition and reportability judgment isn't yours, and shouldn't wait on you to relay it. |
| A quality decision under pressure | Quality leadership | The independence bypass — see below. |
| Suspected breach of donor or patient data | Privacy/security or compliance owner | A different specialty than product quality, with its own clock. |
| Major system or business risk | Your CIO | Yours to decide whether to escalate upward, not to sit on. |
| Anything with legal exposure attached | Legal | A different judgment than regulatory posture, not one to conflate. |

**The independence bypass is a required path, not a nice-to-have.** Every escalation scheme
needs at least one route that doesn't pass through the Director at all — straight to Quality
leadership — because the Director sits inside the same reporting line the pressure sometimes
comes from. If the only way to escalate "someone's telling me not to write this up" is to tell
the person whose chain that pressure might be coming down, the control doesn't exist. Same
independence principle `qa-deliverables-and-ownership` made about disposition authority, now
built into the routing itself instead of just the signature line.

**"Reasonably suggesting," not "confirmed," is the threshold — and this is the load-bearing
idea in this whole module.** 21 CFR 606.171(c) starts FDA's own reporting clock at the moment
someone acquires information *reasonably suggesting* a reportable event occurred, not at the
moment anyone confirms one did. If Lakeshore's internal escalation criteria are written to fire
on "confirmed," they are, by definition, slower than the clock they're supposed to help
Lakeshore meet. Write escalation thresholds to key on *suspected*, on *possibly*, on *may* — the
same word doing the work in 606.171(b)'s "may affect" test you already learned in
`risk-and-controls-vocabulary` — and confirmation becomes something that happens *after*
escalation, during the investigation, not a precondition for it.

**Internal windows have to be tighter than external clocks, or the external clock loses.** If
FDA's outer deadline is 45 calendar days from "reasonably suggesting," and Lakeshore's own
escalation criterion also lets most of 45 days elapse before Director or Quality even hears
about it, there's no time left to investigate, decide, and file. A "call me now" or "tell me
today" window exists to leave room, on Lakeshore's side of the clock, for everything that has to
happen before a filing decision is even possible.

**Escalating informs. It does not transfer the decision.** When your QA calls at 11:52 p.m., she
isn't asking you to decide whether the event is reportable, or what happens to the product.
Disposition and reportability stay exactly where Lakeshore's SOP puts them — the medical director
or a delegated quality officer, the authority `qa-deliverables-and-ownership` and
`reviewing-deviations-and-capas` already established isn't yours. The call buys time: the right
people know sooner, evidence gets preserved sooner, and nobody waits on a write-up that doesn't
exist yet to start acting.

**Under- and over-escalation are both real failures, and they don't cancel out.**
Under-escalation is the obvious one — a fatality call sitting in an inbox until morning.
Over-escalation is quieter: every minor deviation and routine supplier reassessment routed as
"call me now," until the people receiving those calls stop really listening. Alert fatigue is
real in your world already; a QA trained to escalate everything is, in practice, one who's
stopped escalating anything that matters.

**Your own upward criteria to the CIO are part of this, not separate from it.** You're not just
the receiving end of escalation — you're a sender too. Tell your CIO now, not at the weekly
download, when: a BECS critical-function failure has real production exposure; a vendor security
notice touches a system BECS depends on; a quality-blocking disagreement can't get resolved
through Quality's own path and threatens a business deadline; or anything else crosses from "a
system risk I'm managing" into "a business risk my CIO needs to hear from me first."

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| 21 CFR 606.171(c) | "Six-oh-six point one-seventy-one, paragraph c" | The 45-day reporting clock starts on the date information is acquired "reasonably suggesting that a reportable event has occurred" — not on the date it's confirmed. | The regulatory anchor for this whole module: internal escalation has to key on the same word FDA uses, or it will always run behind the clock it's meant to help meet. |
| 21 CFR 606.170(b) | "Six-oh-six point one-seventy, paragraph b" | A fatal complication of blood collection or transfusion must be phoned or electronically reported to FDA "as soon as possible," with a written report within 7 days — filed by the collecting facility for a donor reaction, or by the facility that performed compatibility testing for a transfusion reaction. | Already taught in `storage-distribution-and-hemovigilance`: the filing on tonight's fatality call is very likely Riverside's, not Lakeshore's — and that fact changes nothing about whether tonight's call needed to reach you immediately. |
| 21 CFR 606.100(b)(19) | "Six-oh-six point one-hundred, paragraph b, sub-nineteen" | Written SOPs must include procedures — under §§ 610.46 and 610.47 — for notifying consignees to quarantine affected product. | Named here as the regulatory hook behind "consignee notification or retrieval" as a trigger category. The specific circumstances that activate that duty (610.46/610.47) aren't in this curriculum's sources yet and aren't taught here — this citation tells you the category exists, not how to run it. |

## The actual text

The clock-start language, quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/606.171.md` — the anchor for
everything above:

> (c) *When do I report under this section?* You should report a biological product deviation as
> soon as possible but you must report at a date not to exceed 45-calendar days from the date
> you, your agent, or another person who performs a manufacturing, holding, or distribution step
> under your control, acquire information reasonably suggesting that a reportable event has
> occurred.

The whole module rests on that gap. The clock doesn't wait for proof — it starts on suspicion
that would lead a reasonable person to think a reportable event might have happened, a lower,
earlier bar than most people's instinct for when to escalate. A policy that waits for certainty
is, by definition, waiting past the point FDA's own clock already started running.

The fatality-notification text, quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/606.170.md`, already the
backbone of `storage-distribution-and-hemovigilance`:

> (b) When a complication of blood collection or transfusion is confirmed to be fatal, the
> Director, Office of Compliance and Biologics Quality, CBER, must be notified by telephone,
> facsimile, express mail, or electronically transmitted mail as soon as possible. A written
> report of the investigation must be submitted to the Director, Office of Compliance and
> Biologics Quality, CBER... within 7 days after the fatality by the collecting facility in the
> event of a donor reaction, or by the facility that performed the compatibility tests in the
> event of a transfusion reaction.

Notice this clause's own trigger word is "confirmed" — narrower than 606.171(c)'s "reasonably
suggesting." Not a contradiction; two obligations, two thresholds. 606.170(b)'s external filing
genuinely waits for a confirmed fatality. Lakeshore's *internal* escalation shouldn't wait for
that same confirmation — tonight's call goes out on "a hospital says this might be ours," not on
a confirmed cause of death.

And the consignee-notification hook, quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/606.100.md` — named only,
not developed further:

> (19) Procedures under §§ 610.46 and 610.47 of this chapter: ... (iii) To notify consignees to
> quarantine in-date blood and blood components previously donated by such a donor intended for
> use in another person or for further manufacture into injectable products...

That's as far as this module goes into that clause. What actually triggers this duty — post-
donation testing reactive for HIV or HCV — belongs to sections not yet in this curriculum's
sources. Treat "a consignee notification or retrieval question has come up" as its own trigger
category on its own facts, without needing the lookback mechanics behind it yet.

## The drill: one evening, five calls

Here's the full night behind the call that opened this module — five events, in the order they
actually reached the QA or the on-call supervisor. **Before you read the reveal, sort each one
yourself: now, today, one-on-one, or periodic report — and for the ones that rate "now," decide
who besides you it needs to reach.**

1. **11:52 p.m.** Riverside General Hospital calls the QA directly: a transfusion recipient has
   died, and the unit involved may be a Lakeshore product.
2. **12:40 a.m.** An email arrives from the BECS vendor's security team: they've detected a
   security incident on the remote-support platform their engineers use to service Lakeshore's
   BECS installation.
3. **1:15 a.m.** A voicemail from third-shift: a donor's required callback — a follow-up question
   on a travel-history item — went out a day late. The unit stayed in quarantine the entire time;
   nothing shipped.
4. **2:50 a.m.** An automated alert: a scheduled off-hours BECS configuration change completed,
   but the post-deployment verification check on the label-printer interface just failed.
5. **6:10 a.m., shift change.** The overnight site lead pulls the QA aside before she leaves and
   asks her to "hold off writing up" a temperature excursion from earlier in the shift — nothing
   urgent, he says, just wait until after the weekend so it doesn't complicate the Monday
   inventory count.

### The reveal

**1. The fatality call — now, and past you to the medical director.** Everything
`storage-distribution-and-hemovigilance` taught about who *files* the eventual 606.170(b) report
still holds: if confirmed, that's Riverside's filing, since Riverside performed the compatibility
testing, not Lakeshore's. None of that changes tonight's call. Lakeshore's product is implicated
in a possible death, so it reaches you immediately, and the medical director immediately too —
functionally, because clinical and reportability judgment is theirs, not yours to relay slowly.
"Not our filing" and "not our problem tonight" are different sentences; only the first is true.

**2. The vendor security notice — now, and past you to privacy/security.** A security incident on
the platform the BECS vendor uses to remotely access Lakeshore's system is a suspected breach, and
that's exactly why it can't wait for confirmation. It routes functionally past you to whoever owns
privacy and security review, not just to you as an FYI — and it's a fair candidate for your own
upward call to the CIO before morning, since remote access into a system BECS depends on is
squarely "major system risk," not a routine vendor hiccup.

**3. The late callback — your call, one-on-one.** This is `risk-and-controls-vocabulary`'s
Deviation A: the unit stayed quarantined the entire time by an independent control, nothing
shipped, worst case was a delayed status update. Low severity, contained the whole time, squarely
inside your QA's own decision rights. A 1:15 a.m. call for this one would be the over-escalation
failure mode worth naming, not quietly rewarding.

**4. The BECS verification failure — now, because a critical function is in question.** The
deciding question is the one `becs-in-the-pipeline` already taught: does the failure touch one of
BECS's critical functions — eligibility, release, **labeling**, or disposition? It does. A failed
post-deployment check on the label-printer interface means Lakeshore can't yet say labeling is
behaving the way the validated configuration expects, in real time, while units may still be
moving through the line. That's a validated-state question, and it stays inside your lane as
system owner alongside Quality — it needs you and Quality together, immediately, not past you.
Had the same alert fired outside the four critical functions, "today" would be the honest answer.

**5. The "hold off" request — escalate, and not through you.** A site lead asking the QA to sit on
a temperature excursion write-up is pressure on a quality decision, a trigger category regardless
of how casually it's phrased. What makes this one different: the request came from someone in the
operational chain that sits close to the QA's own reporting line, exactly the situation the
independence bypass exists for. Her correct move isn't to escalate to you and wait — it's the path
that goes straight to Quality leadership, built to exist *before* tonight, so she never improvises
it under pressure. If your only route for "someone's leaning on me" runs through the Director, and
the pressure might be connected to his own chain, the control has already failed by design,
whether or not it fails tonight.

## What an inspector or assessor would actually look for

An assessor doesn't ask whether Lakeshore has an escalation policy — most organizations can
produce one. They ask for evidence it *worked*: timestamps. When did the hospital call, and when
did the medical director's involvement start? A four-hour gap between "possible fatality
reported" and "medical director notified" reads as a control that exists on paper only.

They'll also ask to see the independence bypass exercised, not just described — a real instance
where something got escalated around, not through, the reporting line it would otherwise have
gone through. A policy never once used that way, in an organization where pressure to suppress a
finding is entirely plausible, invites the question of whether it actually exists.

And they'll ask the sharpest version of the "reasonably suggesting" question directly: show me an
event where Lakeshore escalated internally *before* anyone had confirmed what happened. If every
escalation in the file follows a completed investigation instead of preceding one, that's the
finding — a policy structurally too slow for the clock it's supposed to serve.

## Common traps

**Waiting for "confirmed" before picking up the phone.** This is the trap the whole module
exists to break. 606.171(c)'s clock doesn't wait for certainty, and an escalation criterion
written around "once we know for sure" guarantees Lakeshore's internal response is slower than
the deadline it's racing.

**Routing every escalation through the same person, regardless of what's implicated.** A fatality
call, a vendor breach, and a validated-state question don't belong to the same specialist.
"Call the Director" as the universal answer either buries functional experts who should have
heard first, or turns the Director into a bottleneck nobody built him to be.

**No independence-bypass path existing at all.** If the only route for "I'm being pressured not
to write this up" runs through the reporting line the pressure might be coming from, the control
is decorative. Build and test it before the night it's needed, not during it.

**Over-escalating everything, and quietly training people to stop listening.** A QA who calls at
2 a.m. for a Deviation-A-level event is spending trust she'll need the next time it's a fatality
call. Criteria that don't distinguish severity produce exactly the alert fatigue your ITSM world
already knows to guard against.

## What this means for your job

- **Write the four tiers and eight trigger categories down and agree them with Quality before
  you need them at 2 a.m.** — the same criteria-first discipline you already apply to an
  effectiveness check, applied to the moment before any document exists.
- **Check whether your criteria fire on "suspected" or on "confirmed."** If any of them wait for
  confirmation, they're built to lose the race against 606.171(c)'s clock.
- **Know, by name, who a fatality, a breach, a validated-state question, and legal exposure each
  go past you to** — medical director, privacy/security, CIO, legal — and don't let "call me"
  become the default answer for all four.
- **Confirm the independence bypass actually exists and has been used** — not just written down.
  If your QA has never once escalated around you, ask why, before an inspector asks it for you.
- **Set your own upward criteria to the CIO as deliberately as you set hers to you** — a major
  system or business risk shouldn't wait for your weekly download any more than a fatality call
  should wait for morning.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: "FDA requires internal escalation to reach the Director within 24 hours." True or false?

False. FDA sets *external* clocks — 606.171(c)'s 45 days from information "reasonably
suggesting" a reportable event, 606.170(b)'s "as soon as possible" plus 7 days for a confirmed
fatality. Neither clause names an internal window, an hour count, or the Director. Any internal
window is Lakeshore's own policy choice — set tighter than the external clocks not because a
regulation says so, but because there's no time left to investigate and file if the internal
window eats most of the external one.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: Your QA escalates a possible fatality to you and the medical director at the same time, before anyone has confirmed the unit was actually at fault. Has she jumped the gun?

No. Escalating informs; it doesn't transfer the decision. She isn't declaring the product at
fault or making a reportability call — those stay with the medical director and whoever
Lakeshore's SOP names for disposition, as `qa-deliverables-and-ownership` established. She's
making sure the people who *do* own that judgment have the information early, on the same
"reasonably suggesting" threshold 606.171(c) uses. Waiting for confirmation before calling would
be the actual error.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: A different night: a routine supplier's annual reassessment comes back with a minor, already-corrected finding. Your QA calls you about it at 9 p.m. Good escalation discipline, or something else?

Over-escalation. Nothing here fits any of the eight trigger categories — no patient-safety
question, no distributed product, no regulatory clock, no pressure, no BECS critical function.
A minor, already-corrected supplier finding is exactly what "your call, one-on-one," or even
"periodic report," exists for. Calling at 9 p.m. isn't caution — it's the alert-fatigue trap:
every unnecessary "now" call spends trust she'll need the night an event actually warrants one.
:::

## Where this goes next

You now have the routing map: which events reach you immediately, which can wait for today,
which are hers to hold until your one-on-one, and which path exists for the moment someone tries
to keep an event from reaching anyone at all. The next module, `reviewing-validation-packages`,
picks up a document this course has been waiting to finish: the validation impact assessment for
the BECS patch your QA rejected outright back in `becs-in-the-pipeline`. It's scoped to the
decision trail for now — scope, criteria set before testing, approvals in the right order — not
to judging whether the testing itself was technically enough.
